title: Quantum non-Markovian response spectra
authors: Aaron Sander, John F. Kam, Gauthameshwar S., Robert Wille, Kavan Modi
abstract: Quantum systems are rarely isolated from their surroundings. These hidden environments can retain information and return it later, producing correlated errors in quantum computers and complicating the interpretation of experiments.On a quantum processor, for example, one job can therefore leave an environmental trace that affects the next, even after the qubits themselves have been reset. Learning how this hidden influence persists and affects later behavior is therefore important, but the environment is often impossible to measure directly, and fully reconstructing its effects through tomography rapidly becomes impractical. Here, we introduce a response matrix that uses controlled interventions and observations of the system alone to reveal the temporal structure of environmental memory. The matrix records how future observations change across different controlled histories. Its spectrum characterizes how memory is structured and how it persists under specified system resets, while suitable linear combinations of its entries can rule out specified classical models of that memory. Because its history-future queries can be evaluated independently, numerical response matrices can be assembled in parallel. We establish the framework theoretically, characterize response spectra in an interacting spin process, and certify quantum memory in a two-qubit benchmark. This approach turns system observations into a probe of inaccessible environments and could support the diagnosis of correlated noise, tests of open system models, and memory-aware control design.
summary: This paper introduces a response matrix technique to diagnose environmental memory in open quantum systems without requiring full system-environment tomography. By analyzing the spectrum of this matrix, researchers can quantify how past system history influences future measurements across a temporal cut. This offers a practical diagnostic tool for characterizing correlated noise in quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing environmental memory in open quantum systems, where past interactions affect future measurements even after system resets.
main_result: A novel response matrix approach allows for the diagnosis of environmental memory structure by analyzing its spectrum, circumventing the need for full process tomography.
method: The authors introduce a response matrix constructed from controlled interventions and system observations across a causal break, whose spectrum characterizes temporal memory structure.
model_or_system: The framework is applied theoretically to general quantum stochastic processes and benchmarked on interacting spin systems and two-qubit platforms.
key_observables: Response matrix, singular spectrum, response entropy, and quantum-memory witnesses.
important_parameters: The degree of environmental correlation (memory strength $\epsilon$), probe budget ($m$), and environment size.
main_assumptions: The diagnostics are probe-dependent, meaning the detected memory is only characterized for the specific set of measurements performed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of the response matrix across a causal break and show how the response entropy varies with probe budget and environment size.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general theory of quantum stochastic processes to the construction of the response matrix, followed by spectral diagnostics and concrete demonstrations on Ising and two-qubit models.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, operational tool for diagnosing correlated noise and memory effects in open quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding decoherence in quantum computation and simulation.
